name: Foster's Rule
statement: On islands, big animals tend to shrink and small animals tend to grow.
statementAccent: big animals tend to shrink and small animals tend to grow
meaning: Isolated on islands, members of a species evolve toward a different body size than their mainland relatives: large-bodied species tend to become smaller, in insular dwarfism, while small-bodied species tend to become larger, in insular gigantism. Which way a lineage moves depends on the resources and selective pressures the island offers.
mechanism: Several drivers, context-dependent rather than singular. Relaxed predation removes the advantage small prey once gained from being small and cryptic, letting them enlarge. Limited island resources and small land area cap the food supply, selecting large-bodied species downward toward smaller territories, better famine survival, and shorter generations. Released or altered competition reshapes the optimal size. For herbivores competition tends to be the main driver, for carnivores prey availability, so the rule is a family of pressures pointing, on average, in opposite directions for large and small bodies.

examples.text: Pleistocene Mediterranean islands (Sicily, Malta, Crete, Cyprus) carried dwarf elephants, and dwarf hippos lived on several; pygmy mammoths dwarfed on California's Channel Islands. These are the classic, well-supported dwarfism cases.

Small-bodied lineages enlarged on islands: giant rodents, the flightless dodo of Mauritius, and, more contestedly, Komodo dragons and giant tortoises, some of which may be relics of formerly widespread large forms rather than true island-rule cases.

Homo floresiensis, the small-bodied hominin of Flores, is commonly interpreted as insular dwarfism of Homo erectus, though whether it is a dwarfed lineage or a distinct small species remains genuinely debated.

variants.name: Insular dwarfism and gigantism
variants.text: The two halves of the rule, the shrinking of large species and the enlarging of small ones, each robustly documented in particular clades even where the graded rule as a whole is disputed.

variants.name: Island syndrome
variants.text: The broader suite of morphological, ecological, physiological, and behavioural shifts that island populations tend to show, of which body-size change is one part.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most cited generalisations in island biogeography and evolutionary ecology, organising a striking range of fossil and living cases and framing a long-running debate about how island isolation reshapes bodies. Whether or not it holds as a universal rule, it directs attention to the distinctive selective world of islands.

working.lead: Ask which way the pressure points
working.text: for a species colonising an island, weigh relaxed predation, which favours enlarging small species, against limited resources, which favour shrinking large ones.
expect the pattern to hold within particular groups rather than across all animals, since the evidence is strongest at the taxon level.
not every island giant or dwarf is an island-rule effect: some are relics or contested, so verify the case before invoking the rule.

limits: Its generality is genuinely disputed. Applying phylogenetic comparative methods, Meiri, Cooper, and Purvis argued in 'The island rule: made to be broken?' (2008) that there is no evidence for a universal island rule, only clade-specific patterns, with the apparent graded trend an artefact of pseudoreplication, as many small enlarging rodents and many large dwarfing deer create a spurious gradient. A 2021 vertebrate-wide study reached the opposite conclusion, so the debate is live in both directions. Mechanisms are multiple and context-dependent, and several celebrated cases are contested.
misreadings: It is not a law that every island population changes size predictably. It is a contested tendency that holds strongly in some clades and fails in others. And it does not identify a single cause: relaxed predation, limited resources, and altered competition all contribute, differently for herbivores and carnivores.
origin: Described by J. Bristol Foster in 'The evolution of mammals on islands,' Nature 202:234-235 (1964), from a survey of about 116 insular mammal populations; the term 'the island rule' was coined by Leigh Van Valen in 1973.

sources.text: Foster's rule, Wikipedia. — the dwarfism/gigantism statement, the mechanisms, and the Foster 1964 origin.
Meiri, Cooper & Purvis, "The island rule: made to be broken?" Proc. R. Soc. B 275:141-148, PMC. — the phylogenetic critique and the pseudoreplication argument.
